data.title: Serif & Sans
data.tagline: Choose letterforms that match the content and reading task
data.description: Serif typefaces have finishing strokes; sans-serif typefaces do not. Neither is automatically more readable or modern. Choose from the product's tone, text length, language support, and screen sizes, then test real headings and paragraphs.

use: Set a clear tone for headings
Pair two families with distinct roles
Test Chinese and Latin text together when both appear
avoid: Choose a font only because of a style label
Mix several families without clear roles
Use a display face for long body text
Assume one family renders every language equally well

lessonPractice.title: A bilingual editorial site wants serif headings and sans-serif body text. English samples work, but Chinese falls back to browser defaults. What comes next?

options.label: Choose bilingual fonts and fallbacks, then test them with real copy
options.feedback: The style only works when coverage, size, weight, and line-height remain readable, and fallback is part of the system.

options.label: Specify only the English font and let each browser choose its own Chinese fallback
options.feedback: Uncontrolled fallback can create visibly different weight, proportion, and tone across the bilingual page.

options.label: Choose whichever serif or sans font feels best for each heading at the same level
options.feedback: Role-free mixing breaks hierarchy consistency and makes font loading and fallback difficult to maintain.

data.agentPrompt: Create bilingual font rules: use a serif with Chinese coverage or an explicit fallback for headings and a readable sans-serif for body text. Keep peer roles consistent and test real Chinese, English, numerals, bold text, and load failure.
